scenes.name: Malcolm McLaren y Bow Wow Wow
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Tras perder a los Sex Pistols, McLaren se exilia en París, descubre la música africana y, con la moda pirata del siglo XVIII de Vivienne Westwood, concibe su contraataque al postpunk «para universitarios»: ritmos burundeses (Simon Jeffes enseña polirritmia a Adam and the Ants, a quienes luego roba la banda), glamour, sexualidad adolescente y piratería en cassette. Con la anglobirmana Annabella Lwin, de catorce años, nace Bow Wow Wow: «C·30 C·60 C·90 Go!» (1980), Your Cassette Pet, solo en cassette con caja de cigarrillos, «W.O.R.K.» (el paro como liberación: «conviértanse en piratas»). Anticipa el walkman, la world music y la música como banda sonora portátil, pero también manipula y explota a sus músicos (la revista nunca editada Chicken, fotos con menores). See Jungle! (1982) es una obra maestra del pop justo cuando él pierde el interés; «I Want Candy» triunfa en Estados Unidos. Boy George pasa brevemente por el grupo antes de fundar Culture Club.

podcast.title: Co-owner of SEX (later 6) Shop
podcast.body: Vivienne Westwood co-owned a shop, initially named SEX and later known as "6," located in central London. This shop became a crucial hub for the development of the punk aesthetic. "Junto tenía una tienda que sería la tienda 6 que estaría en el centro de Londres."

podcast.title: Collaboration with Malcolm McLaren
podcast.body: Vivienne Westwood co-owned a clothing store in Chelsea, London, with her partner Malcolm McLaren. The store, initially called "Let It Rock," focused on fashion for Teddyboys, bondage gear, and sex toys. After McLaren's pivotal trip to New York, the store was rebranded as "Sex" and became instrumental in popularizing punk fashion by selling garments held together with safety pins, a style inspired by Richard Hell. "Before Malcolm McLaren hooked up with the pistols, he and his partner Vivian Westwood owned a clothing store in the Chelsea area of London called Let It Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5

podcast.title: Early Shop Style Evolution
podcast.body: Her shop initially sold rockabilly clothing. Over time, she began incorporating sadomasochistic elements and blending them with the aesthetic ideas Malcolm McLaren brought back from Richard Hell. This fusion led to the creation of the first punk aesthetic garments. "Donde vendía ropa mas sin andar rocabili y donde tendría ya unas pequeñas inspiraciones un poco de sado mas okismo y un poco mezclando la estética de Richard Hill con las ideas que tenía Vivian Westwood."

podcast.title: Expensive and Copied Clothing
podcast.body: The clothes sold at her shop, SEX (6), were very expensive. Consequently, the Sex Pistols often stole or were given clothes, and many fans resorted to copying her designs at home because they couldn't afford them. "La ropa que vendía Vivian Westwood en la tienda 6 no era tan tan importante o tan relevante porque una tienda como muy muy cara a los 6 pistos muchas veces robaban la ropa de la tienda otra vez se arregalaban y muchos acaban copiando la idea que tenía Vivian Westwood en su casa porque no podían pagarla."

podcast.title: False Claim to Authorship
podcast.body: Vivienne Westwood claimed to be the originator of the punk aesthetic movement. However, this claim was later disproven, as she had imported and adapted ideas initially conceived by Richard Hell. "Vivian Westwood, la diseñadora que yo creo que convirtió el punk como movimiento estético en las pasarelas. También resultó ser una impostora."

podcast.title: Pioneer of Punk on Catwalks
podcast.body: Vivienne Westwood is recognized for bringing the punk movement as an aesthetic to fashion runways and defining its style for a wider consumer audience. "Vivian Westwood, la diseñadora que yo creo que convirtió el punk como movimiento estético en las pasarelas."

xref.title: Band Formation by Malcolm McLaren
xref.body: The Sex Pistols were conceived and formed by Malcolm McLaren, who co-owned the "Sex" shop at 430 King's Road with Vivienne Westwood. McLaren's intention was for the band to serve as a living, breathing advertisement for his store and Westwood's punk clothing designs after they transitioned from selling Teddyboy gear in 1975. "In 1975, Malcolm McLaren and Vivian Westwood had stopped selling clothes to teddy boys, and were now catering to punk kids. It was in this shop that Malcolm McLaren came up with the idea of forming a band that would be a living, breathing advertisement for his store and Vivian's clothing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaboration with Vivienne Westwood
xref.body: Malcolm McLaren co-owned a clothing store in Chelsea, London, with his partner Vivienne Westwood. Initially named "Let It Rock," the store specialized in Teddyboy fashion, bondage gear, and sex toys. Following McLaren's inspiration from Richard Hell, the store was later renamed "Sex" and began selling creations that incorporated safety pins, which became an iconic element of early punk fashion. "Before Malcolm McLaren hooked up with the pistols, he and his partner Vivian Westwood owned a clothing store in the Chelsea area of London called Let It Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5

xref.title: Designed to Showcase Fashion
xref.body: Bow Wow Wow was a group specifically designed by Malcolm McLaren for nothing more than to showcase Vivienne Westwood's new fashions. McLaren continued his trend of intertwining fashion and music with this project.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Life and Fashion Career
xref.body: Born in Yemen and raised by his grandmother in London, Malcolm McLaren attended various art schools before deciding on a career in fashion. He was always a schemer and, along with his girlfriend Vivienne Westwood, opened a shop at 430 Kings Road in London, initially called Paradise Garage in 1971. The shop evolved through names like Too Fast to Live, Too Young to Die and Sex, becoming a hub for unusual clothing, including fetish and bondage gear.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formed in a Clothing Shop
xref.body: The Sex Pistols were formed in a clothing shop owned and operated by Malcolm McLaren and Vivienne Westwood, who were designers specializing in fetish and bondage gear. The band's initial aesthetic was directly inspired by McLaren's observation of New York punk Richard Hell, who used safety pins to hold his decomposing clothes together, a look Vivienne Westwood subsequently introduced in their shop. "A few years later, the sex pistols were formed in a clothing shop run by a couple of designers of fetish and bondage gear."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: High-Profile Modeling Work
xref.body: Her modeling career includes appearances in Italian Vogue and Harper's Bazaar, and she has modeled for prominent brands such as Chanel, Vivienne Westwood, Burberry, Doc Martens, Converse, French Connection UK, and the lingerie line Agent Provocateur. "She's modeled for Chanel, Vivian Westwood, Burberry, Doc Martin's Converse, French Connection UK, and Agent Provocator, the lingerie line."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Richard Hell's Safety Pins – Origin of Punk Fashion Adopted by McLaren and Westwood
xref.body: The punk fashion of wearing safety pins, later popularized worldwide by Malcolm McLaren and Vivienne Westwood, originated with Richard Hell of Television and the Voidoids in New York, who used them out of poverty to hold his torn clothing together. "The punk safety pin fashion was inspired by Richard Hell, who used them out of poverty to hold his clothes together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
